source: Atreya et al. (2026) When to Review: Spaced Repetition for Continual Pre-Training of Language Models
finding: Spaced Repetition Training (SRT) uses SuperMemo-2 review state per example, with per-example perplexity as the recall signal, to pick which old examples return during continual pre-training. It restores old knowledge better than uniform replay at the same replay budget.
numbers: TinyLlama Wikipedia QA, old-knowledge accuracy: base 54.3%, naive continual pre-training (CPT) 11.7%, uniform replay 25.2%, SRT 49.0%. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct: base 50.2%, CPT 43.0%, uniform replay 46.2%, SRT 51.6%. Same 20/80 old/new cap for replay and SRT. New-knowledge accuracy for CPT 17.0% vs base 13.1% on TinyLlama.
quote: scheduling, not exposure, drives SRT's gains
limits: Single preprint, small models (TinyLlama, 3B). Questions auto-generated from source passages and manually checked. Gap over uniform replay shrinks with scale (23.8 points at TinyLlama, 5.4 at 3B).
agent_relevance: Scheduling when an item returns (not just how often) is the active ingredient. A memory or lesson store in our agent should schedule review by how fast an item is forgotten, not replay everything uniformly.

source: Atreya et al. (2026) When to Review: Spaced Repetition for Continual Pre-Training of Language Models (difficulty-only control)
finding: A difficulty-only baseline (replay highest-perplexity old examples, no interval scheduling) learns new facts fastest but keeps less old knowledge. Hardest-first is not the same as spaced.
numbers: Wikipedia: PPL-Prioritised new-knowledge accuracy 38.8% (best of all methods) but old accuracy 27.4% vs SRT 49.0% (21.6-point gap); uniform replay old accuracy 25.2%.
limits: Authors explain this as greedy focus on current hardest items; this is their interpretation, not isolated by ablation.
agent_relevance: Choosing 'hard' items is not enough. The intermediate-difficulty items that are about to be forgotten need revisiting. Guards against an 'always retry the hardest failure' rule.

source: Atreya et al. (2026) When to Review: Spaced Repetition for Continual Pre-Training of Language Models (broad capability harm)
finding: Uniform replay can damage reasoning more than no replay. SRT keeps base-level performance on broad benchmarks.
numbers: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct: CPT drops GSM8K 77.6% to 38.8%; uniform replay drops BBH to 8.4% and GSM8K to 6.8%; SRT stays near base (MMLU 57.8, BBH 52.6, GSM8K 76.7, PIQA 74.3). SRT overhead about +14.7% wall-clock vs CPT.
limits: TinyLlama is near random on MMLU/GSM8K so no signal there. Authors say the mechanism of uniform-replay damage is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Shows 'more practice' can hurt: a naive rehearsal rule can lower broad skill while raising the trained score. Measure transfer, not just the practised item.

source: Janik (2024) Aspects of human memory and Large Language Models
finding: In-context lists of facts: an LLM recalls a fact better when a repeat is separated from the first presentation by intervening text than when the repeat follows right away. Authors say this mirrors human spacing, though there is no obvious reason it should.
numbers: Qualitative (figure only, no exact accuracy numbers in the text I extracted): Fig. 8, repetition after a separation period raises recall over baseline; permuted repetition slightly better than verbatim. Lists of 10-20 facts, 5 repeats per experiment.
quote: Introducing a separation period prior to repetition improves recall.
limits: In-context recall, not weight learning. Exact effect sizes not in the text. Few models.
agent_relevance: A weak sign that spacing of reminders inside a long context matters for a model. Keep similar notes apart or merged, since interference is the main threat to a note kept in context.

source: Janik (2024) Aspects of human memory and Large Language Models (primacy/recency, interference)
finding: LLM serial recall shows primacy and recency (U-shape). Decay with neutral filler is slow. Interference from related distractor facts decreases recall much more than neutral filler. Same-person distractors removed the recency effect.
numbers: Decay test: n repeats of a neutral phrase between a 10-fact list and the query gives only slow decline; related distractor lists (same 10 persons) hurt most. 5 repeated runs per condition.
limits: Descriptive; no statistics quoted in text. Some models (Pythia) lack recency.
agent_relevance: Lessons learned late in a long context compete with similar earlier ones. Supports guardrails that keep working notes short and distinct.

source: Russin, Pavlick & Frank (2024) Human Curriculum Effects Emerge with In-Context Learning in Neural Networks
finding: GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct) and Llama 2 70B show the human blocking advantage on a rule-governed task: better with blocked than interleaved examples in context, and aligned better than misaligned. On a task without a simple rule (rotated) they fail in context.
numbers: Task from Dekker et al. 2022 (25 cues, 9 train, 16 test). Metalearning net trained on 12,000 episodes (100 validation, 10 test). Numbers only in figures; direction: blocked > interleaved in context on the Unrotated task.
quote: ICL explains the observed blocking advantage while concurrent in-weight learning explains the interleaving advantage
limits: Conference paper (CCN), figures only. Fine-tuning (in-weight learning) was tested in small metalearning nets, not in the LLMs (too costly).
agent_relevance: Order of examples in a prompt works the opposite way from in-weight learning: when a rule exists, group related examples in the prompt. Desirable-difficulty advice about interleaving does not carry over to in-context use unchanged.

source: Russin, Pavlick & Frank (2024) (in-weight learning half)
finding: In small metalearning nets that can learn both in context and in weights, interleaving beats blocking only when in-context learning fails and errors flow into weights. Blocked training then causes catastrophic forgetting of the first block.
numbers: Figure 1F: after fine-tuning on the Rotated task, cues trained in block A (TrainA) are forgotten during block B when blocked. One network, two learning systems.
limits: Small synthetic networks; results shown as figures; carrying this to real LLM fine-tuning is the authors' hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism for why interleaving helps weight-trained models and not in-context ones: forgetting. For our no-training scaffold only the in-context half applies.

source: Chen et al. (2026) The Free-Recipe Limit: Every recipe effect measures which premise of an idealised learner broke
finding: Large fine-tuning study (761 runs, 12 base models 0.5B-14B) on competition-math skills. Within one coherent domain at fixed data volume, blocked vs interleaved and order effects are mostly inside run-to-run noise. Winners found by search do not survive reruns.
numbers: Recipe freedoms average 0.010-0.021 against a 0.019 floor; largest contrast 0.0619 reads +0.010 and -0.015 on two reruns. Pair fixed in advance resolves 0.031; pair selected by search resolves 0.144; 2 of 6 pairs reverse sign. About 4 independent runs per endpoint needed to buy resolution back.
limits: Preprint; SFT with AdamW, exact-match scoring, single-valued math answers, base checkpoints. Authors' own framework.
agent_relevance: A caution that matters for us: a single run showing a 'desirable difficulty' win is likely noise. Any claim that a schedule helps needs reruns or pre-fixed comparisons.

source: Chen et al. (2026) The Free-Recipe Limit (interleaving result)
finding: Scored on the capability both skills were trained for, interleaving does beat blocking, and most of the gain is less forgetting of the skill trained first. A last-skill score hides this.
numbers: Gap +0.0483, statistic 8.06 as reported, 6 of 6 pairs, about 2.5 floors; 76% of the gap is forgetting of the first-trained skill. When the pooled corpus holds conflicting answer conventions, arrangement moves allocation by -0.268 and -0.443 vs -0.005 control; Qwen3-8B -0.0875 with all 5 seeds negative.
limits: Math SFT only. Conflict conditions were constructed by the authors. 'Order is a transient whose sign crosses zero three times inside a single run'.
agent_relevance: Matches the human story: interleaving helps retention of earlier skills, but a score taken only on the last item hides it. Test every earlier lesson after each new one.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Beyond Random Sampling: Efficient Language Model Pretraining via Curriculum Learning
finding: Easy-to-hard curricula speed early and mid pretraining, and interleaved-difficulty curricula help for some difficulty measures. Gains depend on the difficulty metric.
numbers: Over 200 models up to 100B tokens, 8 benchmarks. Reaches baseline with 18-45% fewer steps; as warmup before random sampling up to 3.5% sustained gain. Interleaved curriculum helps for compression ratio and number of tokens; others similar or slightly worse. MTLD: +1.8% best performance with 17.9% fewer steps.
limits: Mostly small models; gains are early and mid training; sensitive to metric choice.
agent_relevance: Ordering by difficulty is a real but conditional lever. Easy-first is the opposite of 'desirable difficulty'; the schema should assume neither direction.

source: Elgaar & Amiri (2026) Curriculum Learning for LLM Pretraining: An Analysis of Learning Dynamics
finding: Pythia 14M-1B trained on 300B tokens under three curricula vs random. Curricula change time spent in shared learning phases, not the phases themselves. Effects are larger for small models and smaller at larger scale. Reversing the order loses much of the gain.
numbers: Random ordering gives higher gradient noise scale at 14M-70M; late singular-entropy spikes up to 160M. Descending verb-variation control loses much of the ascending accuracy advantage. Authors note others find negligible effects at scale.
limits: Small models; linguistically motivated curricula only; exact accuracy deltas in figures.
agent_relevance: Easy-first helps constrained capacity. A scaffold used on a strong model may see little from ordering tricks.

source: Mordig et al. (2026) Rethinking Easy-to-Hard: Limits of Curriculum Learning in Post-Training for Deductive Reasoning
finding: On synthetic arithmetic and logic tasks with difficulty defined by reasoning complexity, easy-to-hard ordering shows no robust advantage over random sampling for SFT or RL, in accuracy or response length.
numbers: Model families include Llama3.2-1B/3B, Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B, Gemma2-9B; both SFT and RL; no robust gain over random sampling.
limits: Synthetic deductive tasks; not natural data.
agent_relevance: Evidence against the intuition that an ordered easy-to-hard lesson plan beats a shuffled one for reasoning. Do not build ordering machinery without a measured gain.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2023) Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
finding: Repeating the same data for a few epochs is almost as good as new data. Returns decay with more repetition.
numbers: Up to 4 epochs of repeated data gives negligible loss change vs unique data at fixed compute. Value of repeated tokens has half-life R_D about 15 repetitions (16 epochs); beyond that returns drop fast. Up to 900B tokens, models up to 9B parameters.
limits: Pretraining on web text; repeats were not scheduled by interval, so this is repetition not spacing.
agent_relevance: Repetition has a useful range then saturates. A repeat-until-pass loop in the agent should cap repetitions.

source: Xu et al. (2026) Data-Constrained Language Model Pretraining: Improved Regularization and Scaling Laws
finding: With multi-epoch training, strong weight decay and masked-input regularisation (a harder, noisier objective on the same data) improve validation loss. The SoftQ scaling law models repeated data. Masked-input regularisation is worth about 1.3 times as much unique data.
numbers: 72M-1.4B parameter models; masked-input regularisation beats strong-weight-decay-only baseline on validation loss, downstream gains at 1.4B.
limits: Pretraining setting; 'difficulty' here is objective noise, a loose analogue of desirable difficulty.
agent_relevance: Making a repeated item harder (masking) adds value from the same data. A loose model-side analogue of effortful retrieval.

source: Zucchet et al. (2025) How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
finding: Models learn synthetic biographies in three phases: general statistics, a plateau with no individual knowledge, then knowledge emergence. Imbalanced (Zipf-like) data shortens the plateau. Hallucination appears with knowledge. Fine-tuning on new facts corrupts old memories quickly.
numbers: Plateau length grows almost linearly with number of individuals. Pattern robust over learning rate, weight decay, batch size, model size, attention or recurrent blocks. Imbalance speeds the plateau but slows later acquisition (trade-off).
quote: performance plateaus at the no knowledge baseline
limits: Synthetic task; small models.
agent_relevance: During-learning score can sit flat at the 'no knowledge' level while recall circuits form. A flat early curve is not evidence a lesson failed, another reason not to judge a lesson by immediate gain.

source: Allen-Zhu & Li (2023) Physics of Language Models 3.1: Knowledge Storage and Extraction
finding: A model can memorise facts perfectly and still fail to extract them. Varied rewrites (paraphrase, sentence shuffle, translation) of the same knowledge in pretraining are needed. Without augmentation, extraction accuracy goes to 0%, whatever the later instruction tuning.
numbers: Controlled biography dataset; extraction accuracy tied to diversity measures; 0% without augmentation (abstract). Mixed training with QA for a fraction p of people lets the model generalise to the others.
limits: Synthetic biographies; models trained from scratch.
agent_relevance: The machine version of varied practice: one rote exposure is not learning. Store a lesson in varied forms and test it in a different form from the one learned.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Learning Facts at Scale with Active Reading (Meta FAIR)
finding: Models study a document with self-generated strategies (paraphrase, self-quizzing, association) and are trained on the output. Far more knowledge absorbed than vanilla fine-tuning or other augmentation. The closest machine analogue to retrieval practice and elaboration.
numbers: 8B model: 66% on Wikipedia-grounded SimpleQA subset (+313% relative over vanilla fine-tuning) and 26% on FinanceBench (+160% relative). Table 3: Llama 8B base 7.42; trained on 8B-generated data 66.25; on 70B-generated data 62.26. WikiExpert-8B trained on 1 trillion generated tokens.
limits: Strategies are bundled, so the effect of self-testing alone is not isolated; authors credit data diversity. Llama-family, Wikipedia and finance.
agent_relevance: Study time spent generating questions and varied restatements beats rereading. Supports an operator that makes the agent quiz itself on a note before trusting it.

source: Zhong et al. (2023) MemoryBank: Enhancing Large Language Models with Long-Term Memory
finding: An agent memory store whose items decay by an Ebbinghaus curve R = exp(-t/S). Strength S starts at 1 and rises each time the memory is recalled, so recalled items persist longer. Used in the SiliconFriend companion chatbot.
numbers: Table 2 (three SiliconFriend variants, English and Chinese test sets): retrieval accuracy 0.711-0.856, response correctness 0.418-0.716. No ablation of the forgetting rule in the text I checked.
limits: No test that the forgetting curve itself improves answers; S is a coarse discrete value; human-labelled evaluation.
agent_relevance: The best-known agent-loop use of spacing-style memory strengthening. The benefit of the decay rule is unproven; treat as a design idea, not evidence.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics (PNAS)
finding: Field experiment with nearly 1,000 high-school maths students. Free GPT-4 access (GPT Base) raised practice scores but lowered later unassisted exam scores. A tutor with learning guardrails (GPT Tutor) removed the harm. Students did not notice.
numbers: Practice improvement +48% (GPT Base) and +127% (GPT Tutor). Unassisted exam: GPT Base -0.054 out of 1, i.e. -17% vs control; GPT Tutor -0.004, indistinguishable from control. 2,848 observations in the main regressions; SEs clustered by class.
limits: High-school maths, a few sessions. GPT Tutor did not beat control on the exam despite +127% in practice. A PNAS correction notice and a critique of the design exist (listed in OpenAlex, not read).
agent_relevance: The cleanest AI-era proof that performance during practice misleads. Immediate gain with an assistant (+48%) hid a learning loss (-17%). Strong warning for an agent that grades its own lessons by immediate score.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) (perception result)
finding: Students in the unguarded arm did not perceive that they had learned less. Students in the tutor arm thought they did significantly better although exam scores equalled control. Self-perception was over-optimistic in both arms.
numbers: Copying solutions during practice (regression on practice errors) predicted worse exam results. Perception was survey self-report; magnitudes not extracted here.
quote: they did not perceive that they performed worse or learned less
limits: Self-report survey.
agent_relevance: The metacognitive illusion of Bjork, now measured with an AI helper. An agent's confidence after an easy assisted pass is not a reliable learning signal.

source: Fan et al. (2024) Beware of metacognitive laziness: Effects of generative AI on learning motivation, processes, and performance (BJET)
finding: Randomised study with 117 university students: ChatGPT, human expert, writing-analytics tool, or no tool. ChatGPT improved the essay score most but did not improve knowledge gain or transfer. The ChatGPT group showed fewer metacognitive self-regulation processes.
numbers: Essay score improvement F=4.549, p=0.005, eta2=0.108. Knowledge-gain post-test F=0.913, p=0.438. Transfer F=0.019, p=0.996, eta2=0.000. Interest/enjoyment F=1.087, p=0.358.
limits: One study, short session, essay revision task; the 'laziness' reading of process data is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Bastani with a different task: the visible score rose, the learning did not. Check transfer, not the revised product.

source: Eleftheriou, Pallis & Constantinides (2026) Confidence Without Competence in AI-Assisted Knowledge Work (CHIWORK)
finding: 85 participants, two learning tasks, four LLM designs: standard baseline, future-self explanations, contrastive learning, guided hints. The baseline gave high perceived understanding with the lowest objective learning. Guided hints gave the largest learning gain without more frustration. The authors call the contrastive condition a 'desirable difficulty'.
numbers: Task 2 guided hints vs baseline: statistic 3.64, p=0.002, d=1.14, about 45% improvement in learning outcome, workload unchanged. Contrastive condition had the highest mental demand (mean 4.85); its effect vs baseline d=0.74, p=0.080 (not significant). Future-self condition best matched perceived and actual understanding.
limits: Small groups; preprint; learning measured soon after the task; qualitative themes from interviews.
agent_relevance: Shows prompt design can bring friction back: ask for the user's (or the agent's own) explanation first, give hints rather than answers. Template for a hint-first operator.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
finding: 54 participants wrote essays with an LLM, a search engine, or brain only over 3 sessions; 18 did a 4th session with conditions swapped. EEG connectivity scaled down with external support. LLM users could not quote their own essays minutes later and reported low ownership.
numbers: N=54 (18 per group), 18 completed session 4. LLM-to-brain group had weaker connectivity and under-engagement of alpha and beta networks; brain-to-LLM had higher recall and re-engagement.
limits: Preprint, small N, EEG interpretation debated (a published comment exists, not read); essay writing only.
agent_relevance: Consistent with 'easy help lowers encoding'. Weak evidence alone; use only as support next to Bastani and Fan.

source: Huff & Ulakci (2024) Judgment of Learning: A Human Ability Beyond Generative Artificial Intelligence
finding: Human judgments of learning predicted later memory; GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o judgments did not. LLMs failed to predict human memory from the same sentence pairs.
numbers: 78 human participants (power analysis target about 69). Human JOL slope B=0.104, 95% CI [0.005, 0.202] in the unfitting context; GPT-3.5 B=0.044 CI [-0.087, 0.175]; GPT-4-turbo B=0.016; GPT-4o B=0.027, all CIs include zero.
limits: Cross-agent prediction (LLM predicts human memory), garden-path sentences, recognition test. Not the LLM's own learning.
agent_relevance: Models do not forecast which items humans will find hard to remember. An agent cannot rely on a model's guess of how a lesson will stick; use measured delayed tests.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: A harness elicits a pre-solve feeling-of-knowing and a post-solve judgment-of-learning from the model, then uses them to decide when to trust, retry or aggregate. Applied to Claude Sonnet-4.6 with no training.
numbers: Pooled accuracy 48.3 to 56.9 across HLE-Verified, LiveCodeBench v6 and R-Bench-V text, code and multimodal sets; exceeds the strongest listed leaderboard entries on those three settings.
limits: Preprint; public benchmark snapshots; gains come from a bundle of retry, aggregation and context management, not from the JOL signal alone.
agent_relevance: An existing LLM-agent loop that uses a metamemory signal as control. Self-judgment can help when tied to retry rules, even though Huff finds weak JOL for human memory.

source: Do large language models learn like humans: Interleaved and spaced practice in morphological learning (Acta Psychologica 2025)
finding: Abstract only (via OpenAlex): GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3 and Llama 3.1 beat humans at few-shot learning of artificial verb classes but diverged from human mechanisms. Interleaving helped some models more than blocked under juxtaposition; spacing effects differed from humans; models showed metacognitive illusions (preferring the weaker schedule) or random choices when asked which schedule is better.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract. Interleaving effect for GPT-4o-mini and Llama 3.1; less sensitivity to sequencing in DeepSeek-V3.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract; behaviour is model-dependent.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of spacing and interleaving: human desirable-difficulty results do not transfer cleanly across models, so check any such rule on the chosen model.

source: Winona State symposium talk 'Desirable Difficulties: Configuring Large Language Models for Effective Tutoring' (2026)
finding: Search result only: a talk abstract describes configuring an LLM to give scaffolding, hints and feedback without giving the answer. No results seen.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Abstract only; not a data study.
agent_relevance: Shows the 'desirable difficulty' framing is already used in LLM tutor prompts, but there is no measured result to cite.
